A media company is developing a recommendation engine to boost user engagement by analyzing interactions. They collect and store data like user reviews, ratings, timestamps, and profiles (age, preferences, viewing history). This data is currently stored in a CSV (comma-separated value) format. The company also tracks the names of the content creators, which are stored alongside the interaction data.

Select and order the steps a data scientist could take to optimize the data format and improve processing performance. Each step should be selected one time or not at all. (Select and order THREE.)

Filter out irrelevant columns, focusing only on the reviews, ratings, and timestamps.

Convert the data from CSV format to a hierarchical format such as JSON.

Compress the data to reduce storage requirements and improve processing time.

Keep the data in the existing CSV format and process all columns as-is.

Aggregate the data by content creators’ names.

Transform the CSV data into a columnar storage format for faster access.

Step 1:
(Filter out irrelevant columns, focusing only on the comments, likes, time, and date.)
Step 2:
(Compress the data to reduce storage requirements and improve processing time.)
Step 3:
(Transform the CSV data into a columnar storage format for faster access.)

Incorrect0 / 3 Points
In data science, optimizing data format and storage is critical for improving the performance of machine learning models, especially when working with big and heterogeneous datasets. In instances when an organization wants to adopt a recommendation engine or sentiment analysis model, data processing efficiency can have a substantial impact on the model’s accuracy and responsiveness. This necessitates a deliberate approach to data management, ensuring that only the most important information is processed and that the data is kept in a manner that allows for quick and efficient access.



In the scenario presented, the correct approach consists of three key steps: first, filtering out irrelevant columns to focus on data directly related to user interactions; second, compressing the data to reduce storage space and improve processing speed; and third, transforming the CSV data into a columnar storage format that is optimized for rapid data retrieval. These steps work together to guarantee that the machine learning model runs as efficiently as possible, making the best use of available data while minimizing processing time and storage requirements.

Hence, the correct answers are:

– Step 1: Filter out irrelevant columns, focusing only on the comments, likes, time, and date.

– Step 2: Compress the data to reduce storage requirements and improve processing time.

– Step 3: Transform the CSV data into a columnar storage format for faster access.

The option that says: Convert the data from CSV format to a hierarchical format such as JSON is incorrect because JSON, while flexible and useful for representing complex data structures, is not primarily optimized for the kind of read-heavy operations required in a recommendation engine. JSON’s hierarchical nature can typically lead to increased processing overhead and slower data retrieval compared to columnar formats, making it less suitable for improving performance in this context.

The option that says: Keep the data in the existing CSV format and process all columns as-is is incorrect because CSV is a row-based storage format that is not optimized for large-scale data processing, particularly when only specific columns are relevant to the analysis. Additionally, simply processing all columns without filtering out irrelevant data increases the amount of data that must be handled, leading to slower performance and less efficient data processing.

The option that says: Aggregate the data by content creators’ names is incorrect because the names of content creators are not directly relevant to the recommendation engine’s task of analyzing user interactions with content. Aggregating by content creators’ names would just introduce unnecessary complexity and would not contribute to improving the performance of the recommendation engine, which should focus on user interaction data like reviews, ratings, and timestamps.

question: Transferencia global a S3: subidas y descargas frecuentes de datasets grandes en S3 desde ubicaciones globales, con meta de reducir latencia y acelerar el entrenamiento. ¿Qué servicio recomendar?
options: AWS Global Accelerator, que enruta tráfico TCP/UDP de aplicaciones por la red edge de AWS a endpoints
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, que usa las edge locations de CloudFront para acelerar subidas/bajadas a S3
AWS Direct Connect, enlace dedicado de red privada entre el data center on-premises y la región de AWS
AWS DataSync, agente para copiar grandes volúmenes entre almacenamientos con verificación de integridad
correct_text: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, que usa las edge locations de CloudFront para acelerar subidas/bajadas a S3
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.

El problema: acelerar transferencias a/desde S3 desde clientes distribuidos por el mundo.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Transfer Acceleration enruta el tráfico por las edge locations de CloudFront hasta el bucket, reduciendo latencia en distancias largas.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Global Accelerator: acelera aplicaciones (endpoints TCP/UDP como ALB/EC2), no subidas directas a un bucket S3.
  • Direct Connect: enlace dedicado desde un sitio fijo; no resuelve accesos globales dispersos ni es "sin cambiar el setup".
  • DataSync: orientado a migración/replicación programada, no a acelerar cada subida/descarga interactiva global.
Exam tip "Acelerar hacia S3 desde lejos" = S3 Transfer Acceleration. "Acelerar una app con endpoints" = Global Accelerator.
LinksS3 Transfer Acceleration

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A company is working on optimizing data transfer performance for a large-scale machine learning application. The application involves frequent uploads and downloads of large datasets stored on Amazon S3, which are used for training ML models. These datasets are accessed from various global locations. The goal is to reduce latency and improve transfer speeds to accelerate the training process and deployment of ML models.

Which AWS service should you recommend to achieve this?

AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
AWS Direct Connect
AWS DataSync
Incorrect
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is a feature that operates at the bucket level. It facilitates fast, secure, and straightforward file transfers over long distances between your client and an S3 bucket. The feature is designed to enhance transfer speeds into S3 buckets from around the world. Transfer Acceleration leverages the globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront. When data reaches an edge location, it is directed to Amazon S3 via an optimized network path.



Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration leverages Amazon CloudFront’s globally distributed edge locations to accelerate uploads to Amazon S3. It optimizes data transfer using a content delivery network (CDN) approach. When users upload files, the data is routed through CloudFront’s edge locations, reducing latency and improving transfer speeds.

Hence, the correct answer is: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.

The option that says: AWS Direct Connect is incorrect because this primarily provides a dedicated network connection between on-premises data centers and AWS. However, it’s not specifically designed to optimize S3 data transfers. Its focus is on network connectivity rather than transfer speed.

The option that says: AWS Global Accelerator is incorrect because this only improves application availability and performance by using static IP addresses and anycast routing. It’s not designed for S3 data transfers. Its primary use case is routing traffic to endpoints across regions.

The option that says: AWS DataSync is incorrect because this is used for data migration between on-premises storage systems and AWS services. It doesn’t directly enhance S3 transfer speeds. Its purpose is data synchronization, not acceleration.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html

question: Data lake: una plataforma de e-commerce genera transacciones, imágenes de producto y reseñas. Se requiere almacenamiento seguro, muy durable y altamente disponible. ¿Qué servicio es el más adecuado?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre, sistema de archivos paralelo de alto rendimiento para cargas HPC y de ML
Amazon S3, almacenamiento de objetos con 11 nueves de durabilidad, base típica de un data lake
Amazon EFS, file system NFS elástico compartido entre múltiples instancias EC2 por la red
AWS Storage Gateway, servicio híbrido que conecta almacenamiento on-premises con la nube de AWS
correct_text: Amazon S3, almacenamiento de objetos con 11 nueves de durabilidad, base típica de un data lake
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Amazon S3.

El problema: almacenar grandes volúmenes variados (transacciones, imágenes, texto) de forma segura, durable y disponible: la definición de un data lake.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: S3 ofrece 11 nueves de durabilidad, alta disponibilidad, seguridad y escalabilidad prácticamente ilimitada; es el estándar para data lakes en AWS.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • FSx for Lustre: sistema de archivos paralelo de alto rendimiento (tiene modos scratch y persistente), pero no es un almacén de objetos durable y de bajo costo pensado como base de un data lake; para eso es S3.
  • EFS: file system compartido, más caro y no pensado como base de data lake a escala de objetos.
  • Storage Gateway: integra on-premises con la nube; no es el almacenamiento primario del data lake.
Exam tip "Data lake" en AWS = Amazon S3 casi siempre (durabilidad, escala, integración con Glue/Athena/EMR).

A company is designing a data lake architecture for its large e-commerce platform. The platform generates massive amounts of customer transaction data, product images, and user reviews. The data must be stored securely and ensure high durability and availability.

Which AWS storage service would be the most suitable for this use case?

Amazon FSx for Lustre
Amazon S3
Amazon EFS
AWS Storage Gateway
Incorrect
A data lake built on AWS utilizes Amazon S3 as its main storage platform. Amazon S3 offers an ideal base for a data lake due to its virtually limitless scalability and high durability. You have the flexibility to smoothly increase storage from gigabytes to petabytes of content, and you only pay for what you use. Amazon S3 is designed to provide 99.999999999% durability. It offers scalable performance, user-friendly features, built-in encryption, and access control capabilities. Amazon S3 seamlessly integrates with a wide range of AWS and third-party ISV tools for data ingestion, processing, and security.


Amazon S3 is highly scalable and can handle massive amounts of data. It’s designed for durability and availability, making it suitable for storing customer transaction data, product images, and user reviews. Amazon S3 provides durability for objects stored in it. This means your data is highly protected against loss. It offers high availability across multiple Availability Zones (AZs), ensuring your data remains accessible even if one AZ experiences issues. Amazon S3 supports encryption, access control policies, and fine-grained permissions, allowing you to secure your data.

Hence, the correct answer is: Amazon S3.

The option that says: Amazon EFS is incorrect because it is primarily designed for shared file storage across multiple instances. It lacks the scalability needed for massive data lakes and isn’t optimized for this use case.

The option that says: Amazon FSx for Lustre is incorrect. It’s more suitable for high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, not general-purpose data lakes.

The option that says: AWS Storage Gateway is incorrect because this service only connects on-premises environments to AWS storage services. It’s not intended for building data lake architectures.

question: Métricas de sesgo (Clarify): se quiere comparar la proporción de resultados positivos entre distintos grupos raciales. ¿Qué métrica de sesgo pre-entrenamiento aplica?
options: Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Class Imbalance (CI)
Total Variation Distance (TVD)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL)
correct_text: Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL).

El problema: se compara la proporción de etiquetas positivas entre grupos demográficos.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: DPL mide exactamente la disparidad en la proporción de resultados positivos entre grupos, revelando favoritismo hacia uno.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • CI: mide representación de clases (imbalance), no proporción de resultados positivos entre grupos.
  • TVD: mide la máxima divergencia de distribuciones, no la diferencia de proporciones de etiquetas.
  • KL: compara distribuciones de probabilidad en general; no está hecha para comparar proporciones de etiquetas por grupo.
Exam tip DPL = diferencia de proporción de positivos entre grupos. CI = imbalance de representación. TVD = máxima disparidad de distribuciones.

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A data scientist is in the process of examining a machine learning model to identify potential biases within the training data before it’s deployed in a production environment. The goal is to guarantee that the model exhibits no disproportionate favoritism or discrimination towards any specific demographic group.

Match each pre-training bias metric with its appropriate scenario. Each metric may be used more than once. (Select THREE.)

Total Variation Distance (TVD)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL)
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Class Imbalance (CI)
The data scientist wants to compare the difference in the proportion of positive outcomes among different racial groups.
(Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL))
The dataset must be analyzed to measure the imbalance between male and female instances.
(Class Imbalance (CI))
The data scientist is interested in evaluating the maximum disparity in results among different income levels.
(Total Variation Distance (TVD))


Incorrect0 / 3 Points
Evaluating and reducing bias in machine learning models is crucial for creating fair and accurate models, especially when dealing with sensitive demographic data. Pre-training bias metrics are essential tools for data scientists to identify and address potential biases within a dataset before the model is trained. Applying these metrics can help ensure that machine learning models are more equitable and that predictions do not disproportionately favor or disadvantage specific groups.



Class Imbalance (CI) – This metric evaluates the representation of different classes or demographic groups in a dataset. For instance, if one gender is significantly underrepresented, CI will reveal this imbalance, which could lead to biased predictions that favor the more represented class. Addressing such imbalances is important to ensure that the model learns fairly from all data groups.

Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL) –  DPL measures disparities in the proportion of positive outcomes between different demographic groups. For example, if a model predicts higher success rates for one racial group compared to another, DPL will highlight this discrepancy, indicating a potential bias in outcomes. Analyzing DPL can make adjustments to the model or dataset to reduce such disparities and promote fairness.

Total Variation Distance (TVD) – TVD quantifies the maximum divergence in outcome distributions between different demographic groups. It’s a critical metric for identifying how much the predicted outcomes for one group differ from another, thus helping to assess bias in the model’s predictions.

Hence, the correct answers are:

– The data scientist wants to compare the difference in the proportion of positive outcomes among different racial groups: Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)

– The dataset must be analyzed to measure the imbalance between male and female instances: Class Imbalance (CI)

– The data scientist is interested in evaluating the maximum disparity in results among different income levels: Total Variation Distance (TVD)

The option that says: Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL) is incorrect. This metric primarily measures the divergence between two probability distributions often used to compare the distribution of outcomes across different groups. KL Divergence is not specifically tailored for measuring class imbalance or comparing the proportion of labels across demographic groups. It is typically used in broader contexts of distribution comparisons and might not provide a direct assessment of bias related to demographic attributes.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-measure-data-bias.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-detect-data-bias.html

 

Check out this AWS Machine Learning And AI Cheat Sheets:

https://tutorialsdojo.com/aws-cheat-sheets-aws-machine-learning-and-ai/

question: Métricas de sesgo (Clarify): se debe analizar el dataset para medir el desbalance entre instancias masculinas y femeninas. ¿Qué métrica de sesgo pre-entrenamiento aplica?
options: Class Imbalance (CI)
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Total Variation Distance (TVD)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL)
correct_text: Class Imbalance (CI)
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Class Imbalance (CI).

El problema: medir cuánto está sub o sobrerrepresentado un grupo (hombres vs mujeres) en el dataset.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: CI evalúa la representación de clases/grupos y revela desbalances que podrían sesgar el modelo hacia la clase mayoritaria.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • DPL: mide proporción de resultados positivos entre grupos, no la representación/imbalance del grupo.
  • TVD: mide máxima divergencia de distribuciones de resultados, no el conteo/representación.
  • KL: compara distribuciones en general; no es la métrica de imbalance de clases.
Exam tip "Desbalance de representación entre grupos" (m/f) = Class Imbalance (CI).

question: Métricas de sesgo (Clarify): entre dos grupos (definidos por nivel de ingreso), se quiere una métrica de sesgo pre-entrenamiento que sea una distancia ACOTADA (rango 0 a 1) y SIMÉTRICA entre las dos distribuciones de resultados (mismo valor sin importar qué grupo se tome primero). ¿Qué métrica cumple?
options: Total Variation Distance (TVD)
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Class Imbalance (CI)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL)
correct_text: Total Variation Distance (TVD)
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Total Variation Distance (TVD).

El problema: se pide una distancia entre las distribuciones de resultados de dos grupos que cumpla DOS propiedades concretas: estar acotada en [0, 1] y ser simétrica.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: la TVD es la mitad de la norma L1 entre las dos distribuciones; por construcción queda acotada entre 0 y 1 y es simétrica (TVD(P,Q) = TVD(Q,P)). Cumple exactamente las dos propiedades pedidas.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • DPL: compara la proporción de positivos entre grupos; no es una distancia acotada-simétrica entre distribuciones completas.
  • CI: mide la representación/imbalance del grupo, no la distancia entre distribuciones de resultados.
  • KL: Kullback-Leibler también compara dos distribuciones, pero NO está acotada (puede tender a infinito) y NO es simétrica (KL(P,Q) ≠ KL(Q,P)); por eso queda descartada justamente por las dos propiedades exigidas en el enunciado.
Exam tip El desempate TVD vs KL es por las propiedades: TVD es acotada [0,1] y simétrica; KL no es acotada ni simétrica. Si el enunciado pide "acotada y simétrica" = TVD.

A data scientist is in the process of examining a machine learning model to identify potential biases within the training data before it’s deployed in a production environment. The goal is to guarantee that the model exhibits no disproportionate favoritism or discrimination towards any specific demographic group.

Match each pre-training bias metric with its appropriate scenario. Each metric may be used more than once. (Select THREE.)

Total Variation Distance (TVD)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL)
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Class Imbalance (CI)
The data scientist wants to compare the difference in the proportion of positive outcomes among different racial groups.
(Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL))
The dataset must be analyzed to measure the imbalance between male and female instances.
(Class Imbalance (CI))
The data scientist is interested in evaluating the maximum disparity in results among different income levels.
(Total Variation Distance (TVD))


Incorrect0 / 3 Points
Evaluating and reducing bias in machine learning models is crucial for creating fair and accurate models, especially when dealing with sensitive demographic data. Pre-training bias metrics are essential tools for data scientists to identify and address potential biases within a dataset before the model is trained. Applying these metrics can help ensure that machine learning models are more equitable and that predictions do not disproportionately favor or disadvantage specific groups.



Class Imbalance (CI) – This metric evaluates the representation of different classes or demographic groups in a dataset. For instance, if one gender is significantly underrepresented, CI will reveal this imbalance, which could lead to biased predictions that favor the more represented class. Addressing such imbalances is important to ensure that the model learns fairly from all data groups.

Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL) –  DPL measures disparities in the proportion of positive outcomes between different demographic groups. For example, if a model predicts higher success rates for one racial group compared to another, DPL will highlight this discrepancy, indicating a potential bias in outcomes. Analyzing DPL can make adjustments to the model or dataset to reduce such disparities and promote fairness.

Total Variation Distance (TVD) – TVD quantifies the maximum divergence in outcome distributions between different demographic groups. It’s a critical metric for identifying how much the predicted outcomes for one group differ from another, thus helping to assess bias in the model’s predictions.

Hence, the correct answers are:

– The data scientist wants to compare the difference in the proportion of positive outcomes among different racial groups: Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)

– The dataset must be analyzed to measure the imbalance between male and female instances: Class Imbalance (CI)

– The data scientist is interested in evaluating the maximum disparity in results among different income levels: Total Variation Distance (TVD)

The option that says: Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL) is incorrect. This metric primarily measures the divergence between two probability distributions often used to compare the distribution of outcomes across different groups. KL Divergence is not specifically tailored for measuring class imbalance or comparing the proportion of labels across demographic groups. It is typically used in broader contexts of distribution comparisons and might not provide a direct assessment of bias related to demographic attributes.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-measure-data-bias.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-detect-data-bias.html

question: Migración on-prem a EFS: mover un gran dataset de entrenamiento desde servidores on-premises a Amazon EFS, con mínima interrupción y manejo eficiente de grandes volúmenes. ¿Qué servicio es el mejor?
options: AWS Transfer Family, que expone un endpoint SFTP hacia Amazon EFS para que los servidores on-premises suban archivos uno a uno
AWS Storage Gateway en modo File Gateway, que cachea localmente y sincroniza los archivos con Amazon EFS de forma continua
Montar el EFS por VPN y copiar los archivos con rsync desde los servidores on-premises en una ventana de mantenimiento
AWS DataSync, transferencia administrada y paralela on-premises a Amazon EFS con verificación de integridad y mínima interrupción
correct_text: AWS DataSync, transferencia administrada y paralela on-premises a Amazon EFS con verificación de integridad y mínima interrupción
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - AWS DataSync.

El problema: migrar un gran dataset on-premises a Amazon EFS una sola vez, rápido, con integridad y mínima interrupción. Varias opciones tocan EFS; hay que elegir la de migración administrada.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: DataSync copia datos on-premises a EFS (también S3/FSx) en paralelo y a alta velocidad, con verificación de integridad y programación automática, ideal para un traslado masivo puntual.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Transfer Family (SFTP a EFS): también escribe a EFS, pero está pensado para flujos SFTP archivo a archivo, no para copiar en paralelo un dataset enorme con verificación; sería lento.
  • Storage Gateway File Gateway: mantiene una caché local sincronizada de forma continua con AWS; sirve para acceso híbrido permanente, no para una migración masiva de una sola vez.
  • rsync por VPN a EFS montado: funciona y llega a EFS, pero es un proceso manual, sin paralelismo ni verificación administrada, con más riesgo e interrupción que DataSync.
Exam tip Migración administrada on-prem -> EFS/S3/FSx con verificación y mínima interrupción = AWS DataSync. Acceso híbrido continuo = Storage Gateway.

question: Transformar JSON con menor esfuerzo: procesar grandes volúmenes de JSON en S3 para entrenamiento, con una solución automatizada y de mínimo esfuerzo operativo. ¿Qué enfoque conviene?
options: Crear un clúster EMR y usar Apache Drill para transformar el JSON a un formato apto para ML
Usar AWS Step Functions para orquestar varias funciones Lambda que procesen el JSON por lotes
Configurar una Lambda disparada por eventos S3 que procese y transforme el JSON con Pandas a medida
Configurar un job de AWS Glue y usar el editor visual de ETL para transformar el JSON de S3

answer_html:

El problema: transformar JSON a gran escala con mínimo esfuerzo operativo y de forma automatizada.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Glue es ETL serverless y su editor visual permite construir la transformación sin gestionar servidores ni escribir mucho código.

A data analytics team needs to process and prepare large volumes of JSON data from an Amazon S3 bucket for machine learning training. The team requires an automated solution that minimizes operational effort for transforming the data into a format suitable for ML models.

Which approach would best meet these requirements?

Create an Amazon EMR cluster. Use Apache Drill to transform the JSON data into a format for ML models.
Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multiple AWS Lambda functions for batch processing the JSON data.
Set up an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 events. Process and transform the JSON data using Pandas.
Set up an AWS Glue job and use the visual ETL editor to transform the JSON data from S3 for data ingestion.

AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service that makes it easy for analytics users to discover, prepare, move, and integrate data from multiple sources. You can use it for analytics, machine learning, and application development. It also includes additional productivity and data ops tooling for authoring, running jobs, and implementing business workflows.

aws-glue-studio-visual-etl

Glue provides a visual ETL editor that provides an automated way to handle the ETL processes, allowing users to transform data with minimal operational effort. It supports various data formats, including JSON, and can directly read data from Amazon S3. This makes it well-suited for handling large volumes of data and preparing it for ML models.

Hence, the correct answer is: Set up an AWS Glue job and use the visual ETL editor to transform the JSON data from S3 for data ingestion.

The option that says: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multiple AWS Lambda functions for batch processing the JSON data is incorrect because this option introduces additional complexity due to the orchestration of multiple compute functions. While this approach is possible, it is simply not as efficient as using Glue for large-scale data transformations.

The option that says: Set up a Lambda function triggered by S3 events. Process and transform the data for feature engineering using Pandas is incorrect because an AWS Lambda function is subjected to a maximum execution time of 15 minutes. Handling large datasets primarily requires splitting the data or optimizing processing to fit within this limit, making this option less suitable for heavy ETL tasks.

The option that says: Create an Amazon EMR cluster. Use Apache Drill to transform the data into a format suitable for the ML models is incorrect because Amazon EMR is powerful for large-scale processing but is only recommended when you need deep, cluster-level control. It requires far more operational management and configuration compared to the automated, serverless features of Glue.

question: SageMaker 403 a S3: un Processing job conecta al bucket pero recibe 403 al leer los .csv. El bucket existe y el job usa un VPC endpoint. ¿Cuál es la causa más probable?
options: El usuario IAM que creó el Processing job no tiene permisos de administrador en la cuenta
El execution role asociado al Processing job carece de permisos para acceder al bucket S3
La política del bucket S3 deniega explícitamente el acceso al Processing job en cuestión
El bucket S3 está en una región de AWS distinta a la del Processing job de SageMaker
correct_text: El execution role asociado al Processing job carece de permisos para acceder al bucket S3
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Al execution role le faltan permisos sobre el bucket.

El problema: un 403 es de autorización. El Processing job actúa con su execution role (no con el usuario que lo creó).

Por qué la respuesta sirve: si ese role no tiene s3:GetObject/ListBucket sobre el bucket, S3 responde 403 aunque la conexión (VPC endpoint) funcione.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Usuario sin admin: el job usa el execution role, no los permisos del usuario creador; además no se requiere admin.
  • Bucket policy deniega: un Deny explícito en la bucket policy sobre s3:GetObject también produciría el mismo 403 al leer los .csv, pero es menos frecuente: requiere que alguien haya escrito ese Deny concreto. Lo típico es que al execution role le falten s3:GetObject/ListBucket (o kms:Decrypt si hay CMK), por eso es la causa más probable.
  • Región distinta: eso no produce 403 sino errores de resolución/redirección; y como conecta, no es el caso.
Exam tip 403 de SageMaker hacia S3 = casi siempre el execution role sin s3:GetObject/ListBucket (o kms:Decrypt con CMK); un Deny en bucket policy también da 403 pero es menos común. 404 = no existe. Timeout = red/VPC.

An ML engineer sets up an Amazon SageMaker Processing job that fetches .csv files within an Amazon S3 bucket. Although the job successfully connects to the S3 bucket, it encounters a 403 error when attempting to retrieve the .csv files. The ML engineer confirms that the S3 bucket exists and the SageMaker Processing job is correctly configured to use a VPC endpoint.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this error?

The IAM user who created the SageMaker Processing job does not have administrative permissions.
The execution role associated with the SageMaker Processing job lacks the required permissions to access the S3 bucket.
The S3 bucket policy denies access to the SageMaker Processing job.
The S3 bucket is located in a different AWS region from the SageMaker Processing job.
Incorrect
Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs allow ML engineers to perform data preprocessing, postprocessing, and model evaluation using fully managed infrastructure. These jobs typically involve reading data from Amazon S3, performing operations on that data, and then writing the results back to S3. For SageMaker Processing jobs to function correctly, the execution role associated with the job must have appropriate permissions to access the S3 bucket where the data is stored.

In this scenario, the SageMaker Processing job can connect to the S3 bucket, but it encounters a 403 error when trying to access the specific .csv files. A 403 error indicates that the job is being denied access to the files due to insufficient permissions.

Amazon SageMaker Execution Role

The most likely cause of the error is that the SageMaker Processing job execution role does not have the necessary permissions to access the files in the S3 bucket. For the job to successfully access and process the .csv files, the execution role must have appropriate permissions, such as s3:GetObject, to read the files. If these permissions are missing, the job will fail with a 403 error, indicating that access is denied.

Additionally, if the S3 bucket were encrypted with a customer-managed key, the execution role would also need kms:Decrypt permissions, and potentially kms:CreateGrant if the job needs to delegate permissions to SageMaker services.

Hence, the correct answer is: The execution role associated with the SageMaker Processing job lacks the required permissions to access the S3 bucket.

The option that says: The S3 bucket policy denies access to the SageMaker Processing job is incorrect because the scenario describes that the SageMaker Processing job can successfully connect to the S3 bucket. If the S3 bucket policy were denying access, the connection itself would fail, and the job would not even begin to access the files. The error encountered is at the file retrieval stage, indicating that the issue lies with the specific object-level permissions rather than the bucket policy.

The option that says: The S3 bucket is located in a different AWS region from the SageMaker Processing job is incorrect because it can only access S3 buckets across regions, and the bucket’s location alone would not cause a 403 error.

The option that says: The IAM user who created the SageMaker Processing job does not have administrative permissions is incorrect because the permissions of the IAM user who created the job do not directly affect the job’s execution. The job operates based on the permissions granted to its execution role, not the creator’s IAM permissions.

question: Datos supervisados con menor esfuerzo: reseñas crudas sin etiquetar en S3. Antes de poder entrenar un modelo propio de análisis de sentimiento en SageMaker, hay que anotar/etiquetar cada reseña (positivo/negativo/neutral) con alta calidad para producir el dataset supervisado (no se busca clasificar el sentimiento directamente con un servicio ya entrenado). ¿Qué solución logra ese etiquetado con mínimo esfuerzo?
options: Usar el algoritmo Neural Topic Model (NTM) de SageMaker para organizar automáticamente los datasets
Crear un labeling job con SageMaker Ground Truth para anotar las reseñas con alta calidad
Entrenar una red neuronal convolucional (CNN) desde cero para categorizar automáticamente las reseñas
Usar Amazon Comprehend para analizar y clasificar el sentimiento de las reseñas directamente
correct_text: Crear un labeling job con SageMaker Ground Truth para anotar las reseñas con alta calidad
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Labeling job con SageMaker Ground Truth.

El problema: se necesitan etiquetas de alta calidad para datos crudos; Ground Truth es el servicio de etiquetado administrado de SageMaker.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Ground Truth orquesta el etiquetado (humano y asistido) con flujos listos, generando anotaciones consistentes con poco esfuerzo operativo.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • NTM: descubre tópicos, no etiqueta sentimiento; no produce las anotaciones supervisadas necesarias.
  • CNN desde cero: requiere datos ya etiquetados y mucho esfuerzo; no resuelve el etiquetado inicial.
  • Comprehend: clasifica sentimiento, pero el requisito es etiquetar el dataset para entrenar un modelo propio en SageMaker, no inferir directo.
Exam tip "Etiquetar/anotar datos" = SageMaker Ground Truth. "Analizar sentimiento ya, sin entrenar" = Comprehend.

An e-commerce company stores a large dataset of raw customer reviews in Amazon S3. The goal is to develop a text classification system that categorizes reviews into positive, negative, and neutral sentiments. Efficient labeling of the reviews and high-quality annotations are needed to train a sentiment analysis model on Amazon SageMaker AI.

Which solution will achieve this goal with minimal operational effort?

Use the Amazon SageMaker Neural Topic Model (NTM) algorithm to organize the datasets.
Create a labeling job using SageMaker Ground Truth to annotate the reviews.
Train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to automatically categorize the reviews.
Utilize Amazon Comprehend to analyze and categorize sentiment.
Incorrect
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth is a data labeling service that simplifies the creation of high-quality training datasets for machine learning (ML) models. Ground Truth offers a unique combination of automated data labeling and human labeling to ensure efficiency and accuracy. By using active learning, Ground Truth can reduce the manual labeling required by automatically labeling data when it has high confidence in the predictions.

labeling-jobs

SageMaker Ground Truth has a major advantage in handling various data types, such as text, videos, images, and 3D point clouds. The service seamlessly integrates with Amazon S3 for easy data access and provides built-in support for labeling tasks like text classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Moreover, Ground Truth continually enhances its labeling models by incorporating feedback from human labelers, ensuring the accuracy of automated labels. This feature is vital for ensuring that the labeled data is of high quality, making it essential to developing reliable and effective ML models.

Hence, the correct answer is: Create a labeling job using SageMaker Ground Truth to annotate the reviews.

The option that says: Train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to automatically categorize the reviews is incorrect. While CNNs can be used for text classification, the primary need here is to label the raw data first. Training a model requires a labeled dataset, which does not yet exist.

The option that says: Use the SageMaker Neural Topic Model (NTM) algorithm to organize the datasets is incorrect. Neural Topic Model (NTM) is only for unsupervised learning and is used to group documents into topics, not for sentiment classification. It doesn’t help with labeling reviews by sentiment (positive, negative, neutral), nor does it directly support creating labeled datasets for training a model.

The option that says: Utilize Amazon Comprehend to analyze and categorize sentiment is incorrect. Although Amazon Comprehend can provide quick sentiment analysis results, it’s not focused on labeling the data for future use in training custom models. If the goal is to label data for training purposes, Comprehend won’t provide the labeled dataset needed for training your own SageMaker model.

question: Split cronológico: datos ordenados por fecha de alta; el split train/validation debe preservar estrictamente el orden temporal para evitar fuga de datos futuros y overfitting. ¿Qué transform de Data Wrangler usar?
options: Usar el transform Ordered split de Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler para respetar el orden temporal
Ejecutar un script Python en un SageMaker Processing job para dividir el dataset por una clave
Usar el transform Stratified split de Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler para balancear clases al dividir
Usar una receta de AWS Glue DataBrew para realizar un split aleatorio (randomized) del dataset
correct_text: Usar el transform Ordered split de Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler para respetar el orden temporal
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Ordered split en SageMaker Data Wrangler.

El problema: en datos temporales, mezclar el orden filtra información del futuro al entrenamiento (data leakage) y da métricas engañosamente optimistas.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: el Ordered split divide respetando la secuencia (entrena con el pasado, valida con el futuro), evitando la fuga.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Script en Processing job: aunque un script en un Processing job podría transformar datos, el escenario exige una herramienta VISUAL dedicada de preparación sin código, por lo que el script queda descartado por requerir desarrollo manual y no cumplir el requisito de mínimo esfuerzo.
  • Stratified split: preserva proporción de clases, no el orden temporal; puede reordenar y filtrar futuro.
  • Split aleatorio en DataBrew: lo aleatorio rompe la cronología, justo lo que se quiere evitar.
Exam tip Series de tiempo -> Ordered split (nunca aleatorio) para no filtrar el futuro al pasado.
LinksData Wrangler: splits

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A data scientist is working on a machine learning project to predict customer churn using customer demographics, interaction history, and subscription details from the past five years. The goal is to build an ML model that generalizes well to new customers and reduces prediction bias.

The data scientist needs to use an AWS visual data preparation tool to prepare the data and split it into training and validation sets, with the dataset sorted by customer signup date. To prevent future data from leaking into the training set and causing severe overfitting, the split process must strictly preserve the chronological order of the records. If this sequence is disrupted, the resulting ML metrics during validation will be misleadingly optimistic and will not reflect the model’s actual real-world performance.

Which data preparation approach will best meet the requirements?

Use the Ordered split transform in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.
Run a Python script using an Amazon SageMaker Processing job to split the dataset by key.
Use the Stratified split transform in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.
Use an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe to perform a randomized split on the dataset.
Incorrect
With SageMaker Data Wrangler, splitting your data into training, test, and validation sets is now a seamless process that can be done with just a few clicks. This functionality eliminates the need for manual coding, which was previously required to prepare datasets for machine learning model training. SageMaker Data Wrangler provides several split types, including randomized, ordered, stratified, and key-based splits, allowing you to customize how much data is allocated to each split. This feature ensures that your data is properly segmented for downstream ML model training and validation.

Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler Ordered Split

The Ordered split transform in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler is the most suitable choice when working with time-sensitive data, such as datasets sorted by date. This transform ensures that the data is split in the same order as it is provided, preserving the temporal sequence of events. This is particularly important for training machine learning models where the goal is to predict future events based on past data. By using an ordered split, the model is trained on older data and validated on more recent data, mimicking how the model will perform on unseen, future data, and reducing the risk of data leakage.

Hence, the correct answer is: Use the Ordered split transform in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

The option that says: Use an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe to perform a randomized split on the dataset is incorrect because a randomized split divides the data without properly preserving the chronological order. While DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool, a randomized split approach might be generally suitable for typical cases but is simply not appropriate for time-series or date-based data where the sequence of events is crucial for making accurate predictions.

The option that says: Run a Python script using an Amazon SageMaker Processing job to split the dataset by key is incorrect because a key-based split is only meant for partitioning based on a specific key identifier, and it does not ensure that the ML model will generalize well on time-ordered data. Furthermore, using a Python script in a SageMaker Processing job is not a visual data preparation approach, failing the scenario’s requirement.

The option that says: Use the Stratified split transform in Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler is incorrect. A stratified split is typically used only to ensure that each split represents the overall dataset proportionally across a specified key, such as class labels in classification tasks. This method ensures all categories of data are represented in each set but does not handle time series data appropriately.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/06/split-data-train-test-sets-amazon-sagemaker-data-wrangler/

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/create-train-test-and-validation-splits-on-your-data-for-machine-learning-with-amazon-sagemaker-data-wrangler/

question: Migración MySQL a Aurora: hacer una migración puntual (one-time) de datos de entrenamiento de un MySQL on-premises a Amazon Aurora (compatible con MySQL). ¿Cuál es el enfoque más adecuado?
options: Usar AWS DMS para una migración homogénea (MySQL a Aurora MySQL, motores compatibles) de forma administrada
Usar AWS DMS con Schema Conversion Tool para una migración heterogénea convirtiendo el esquema de origen
Exportar el MySQL a un volcado en Amazon S3 y cargarlo en Aurora con sentencias LOAD, orquestando el proceso a mano
Definir un job de AWS Glue que lea el MySQL por JDBC y escriba las tablas en Aurora en una única corrida por lotes
correct_text: Usar AWS DMS para una migración homogénea (MySQL a Aurora MySQL, motores compatibles) de forma administrada
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - AWS DMS, migración homogénea.

El problema: MySQL y Aurora MySQL son motores compatibles: es una migración homogénea puntual, que DMS realiza administrada con mínimo esfuerzo.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: AWS DMS migra esquema y datos entre motores compatibles con mínima interrupción y sin código a medida, que es lo más adecuado para un traslado one-time.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • DMS + Schema Conversion Tool (heterogénea): SCT es para motores distintos (p.ej. Oracle a Aurora); aquí origen y destino son MySQL-compatibles, así que convertir el esquema es un paso innecesario.
  • Export a S3 + LOAD manual: técnicamente logra el one-time, pero es un proceso manual en varios pasos, sin la gestión de esquema, reintentos y validación que DMS ofrece de serie.
  • Job de AWS Glue por JDBC: Glue es un ETL de transformación; para una migración directa entre motores compatibles añade complejidad y no aporta sobre la migración administrada de DMS.
Exam tip Motores compatibles = migración homogénea con DMS. Motores distintos = DMS + Schema Conversion Tool (heterogénea).

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A startup uses an on-premises MySQL database to store its machine learning (ML) model training data. The decision has been made to migrate the ML data to Amazon Aurora for better scalability and performance.

What is the most suitable approach for migrating ML data from MySQL to Aurora?

Use AWS DMS to perform a homogeneous migration from MySQL to Aurora.
Use AWS Data Transfer Terminal by reserving time at an AWS facility and physically connecting equipment to transfer the ML data into AWS, then load it into Aurora.
Set up a real-time data replication pipeline between MySQL and Aurora using AWS DMS.
Create a custom Python script that extracts the ML data from MySQL, compresses it, and uploads it directly to Aurora via the AWS SDK.
Incorrect
The AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) is a managed migration and replication service that helps you quickly and securely move your database and analytics workloads to AWS with minimal downtime and zero data loss. AWS DMS supports migration between over 20 database and analytics engines. For example, you can migrate from Oracle to Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, MySQL to Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, MongoDB to Amazon DocumentDB with MongoDB compatibility, Oracle to Amazon Redshift, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).

AWS DMS

Homogeneous data migrations are serverless and enable you to transfer data between identical database engines. This means you can move data from a MySQL instance to an Aurora MySQL instance. Homogeneous data migrations allow you to migrate data, table partitions, data types, and secondary objects like functions and stored procedures.

Hence, the correct answer is: Use AWS DMS to perform a homogeneous migration from MySQL to Aurora.

The option that says: Use AWS Data Transfer Terminal by reserving time at an AWS facility and physically connecting equipment to transfer the ML data into AWS, then load it into Aurora is incorrect because AWS Data Transfer Terminal is primarily designed for bulk offline data uploads at secure AWS facilities using high-throughput connections. It is not intended for structured database migrations into Aurora. While valid for large unstructured datasets, it does not handle schema conversion, relational integrity, or replication required for database migration.

The option that says: Set up a real-time data replication pipeline between MySQL and Aurora using AWS DMS is incorrect. Although AWS DMS also supports real-time data replication using change data capture (CDC) from source to target, it’s not the best fit for ML data migration. Continuous synchronization can introduce latency and potential data consistency issues. AWS DMS is typically suited for one-time migrations, ensuring consistency during the transition.

The option that says: Create a custom Python script that extracts the ML data from MySQL, compresses it, and uploads it directly to Aurora via the AWS SDK is incorrect. While custom scripts can be used, they require additional development effort and may not handle all edge cases. AWS DMS provides a more robust and straightforward solution for ML data migration.

question: Acelerar subida a S3: un dataset recolectado desde varias ubicaciones sube lento a S3. Se busca acelerar sin cambiar mucho el setup actual. ¿Qué solución es más efectiva?
options: Usar S3 Transfer Acceleration, que enruta la subida por edge locations sin cambiar el flujo hacia el bucket
Usar AWS Data Transfer Terminal, migración física offline en una instalación de AWS con equipo propio
Utilizar AWS Direct Connect, un enlace de red dedicado y privado desde un sitio fijo hacia la región de AWS
Usar Amazon S3 multipart upload estándar, subiendo el dataset en partes en paralelo pero sin acelerar por edge
correct_text: Usar S3 Transfer Acceleration, que enruta la subida por edge locations sin cambiar el flujo hacia el bucket
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - S3 Transfer Acceleration.

El problema: acelerar subidas globales a S3 con cambios mínimos.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Transfer Acceleration solo requiere activarlo en el bucket y usar el endpoint acelerado; enruta por edge locations reduciendo latencia sin rehacer el pipeline.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Data Transfer Terminal: transferencia física, un cambio grande de proceso; no es "sin cambiar el setup".
  • Direct Connect: enlace dedicado desde un sitio fijo; no ayuda a múltiples ubicaciones dispersas ni es cambio mínimo.
  • Multipart upload estándar: paraleliza la subida en partes, lo que ayuda con archivos grandes, pero sigue viajando por la ruta pública de internet; no aprovecha las edge locations, así que ante alta latencia desde ubicaciones lejanas rinde peor que Transfer Acceleration.
Exam tip "Acelerar S3 con mínimos cambios" = S3 Transfer Acceleration (solo activar y usar el endpoint acelerado).

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
An ML specialist uploads a training dataset collected from multiple geographic locations to an Amazon S3 bucket. The current upload process is significantly slower than expected. The specialist seeks a solution to accelerate the data transfer without significantly changing the existing setup.

Which solution will most effectively speed up the upload process to S3?

Use S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Use AWS Data Transfer Terminal.
Utilize AWS Direct Connect.
Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to encrypt and compress the data for faster transfer.
Incorrect
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is a service that speeds up data transfers to Amazon S3 by routing data through Amazon CloudFront’s globally distributed edge locations. This service is beneficial for applications with users spread across different locations or for uploading large amounts of data. Using CloudFront’s optimized network paths, Transfer Acceleration can significantly reduce latency and improve upload performance compared to standard Amazon S3 data transfer methods. The service directs data to the closest edge location, from where it travels over AWS’s optimized network to the target S3 bucket, making the process faster and more efficient without requiring changes to the existing application.

S3 Transfer Acceleration

S3 Transfer Acceleration is easy to enable and requires minimal configuration changes. It is beneficial when end users are far from the S3 bucket’s region or network conditions are suboptimal. Additionally, S3 Transfer Acceleration is compatible with multipart uploads, making it an effective solution for large-scale uploads. The service can be turned on via the S3 console, AWS CLI, or API, and users can easily measure the potential speed improvement using the S3 Transfer Acceleration Speed Comparison tool. This service is a cost-effective way to enhance the performance of data transfers to S3 without the need for complex infrastructure changes.

Hence, the correct answer is: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration.

The option that says: Utilize AWS Direct Connect is incorrect. This service only creates a private connection from your on-premises infrastructure to AWS, bypassing the public internet. While it can offer lower latency and more consistent network performance, it’s best for long-term, high-volume data transfers between a specific location and AWS.

The option that says: Use AWS Data Transfer Terminal is incorrect because this service is intended for offline bulk data transfers using physical devices. It is not designed for continuous uploads from multiple geographic sources.

The option that says: Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to encrypt and compress the data for faster transfer is incorrect. AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) is typically used for creating and controlling cryptographic keys to encrypt data, not for accelerating data transfer speeds.

question: Escalado con outliers: en Data Wrangler, features con rangos muy distintos y outliers en CreditScore (valores atípicos tan bajos como 5). Hay que escalar todo a rango similar siendo robusto a outliers. ¿Qué función usar?
options: Robust Scaler, que escala con mediana y rango intercuartil (IQR), resistente a valores atípicos
Standard Scaler, que centra en la media y divide por la desviación estándar de cada feature
Min-Max Scaler, que reescala linealmente cada feature al rango [0,1] tomando el valor mínimo y máximo
L1 normalization, que escala cada vector para que la suma de los valores absolutos sea igual a uno
correct_text: Robust Scaler, que escala con mediana y rango intercuartil (IQR), resistente a valores atípicos
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Robust Scaler.

El problema: hay outliers que distorsionan media y desviación. Se necesita un escalado robusto.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Robust Scaler usa mediana e IQR (rango intercuartil), estadísticos poco sensibles a valores extremos, por eso resiste outliers.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Standard Scaler: usa media y desviación, ambas muy afectadas por outliers.
  • Min-Max Scaler: reescala linealmente al rango [0,1] pero es muy sensible a outliers (un valor extremo comprime el resto), por eso no es lo adecuado cuando hay outliers; el método robusto usa mediana e IQR.
  • L1 normalization: normaliza la magnitud del vector, no maneja outliers por feature en escalado a rango comparable.
Exam tip Outliers presentes -> Robust Scaler (mediana + IQR). Sin outliers -> Standard/Z-score suele bastar.
LinksData Wrangler: transform numérico

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A data scientist is using Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to prepare a financial dataset for a machine learning model that predicts loan defaults. The dataset has two features: LoanAmount, which ranges from $1,000 to $500,000, and CustomerAge, which ranges from 18 to 75. In addition, the dataset contains a CreditScore feature, with values ranging from 600 to 800 and a few outliers as low as 5. To ensure the machine learning model performs optimally, all features must be scaled to a similar range.

Which scaling function in SageMaker Data Wrangler is most appropriate for addressing the outliers in the dataset?

Standard Scaler
Z-score normalization
Robust Scaler
L1 Normalization
Incorrect
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a variety of scaling methods to normalize features for machine learning models. When dealing with outliers, Robust Scaler is very effective because it scales features using outlier-tolerant statistics. Specifically, it removes the median and scales the data using the interquartile range (IQR), making it less vulnerable to outliers than the Standard Scaler or Min-Max Scaler.

The Robust Scaler modifies the dataset by removing the median and scaling the data based on a predetermined quantile range, regularly the interquartile range (IQR), which spans the first and third quartiles. This method is similar to the Standard Scaler, except instead of using the mean and standard deviation, it utilizes the median and quantiles. This distinction makes it more resistant to the effects of outliers.

TD Robust Scaler

Robust Scaler is especially suited for this scenario since the CreditScore feature has significant outliers (values as low as 5), and using a method sensitive to outliers could adversely affect model performance.

Hence, the correct answer is: Robust Scaler.

Standard Scaler is incorrect because it simply standardizes features by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance, which may not handle outliers effectively, as outliers can significantly affect the mean and variance.

L1 Normalization is incorrect. L1 normalization primarily scales samples so that the sum of absolute values is 1, which does not inherently address the issue of outliers in the feature range.

Z-score normalization is incorrect because it is typically used to scale feature vectors to have a unit norm, but it doesn’t address the issue of outliers in the dataset effectively.

question: Convertir a RecordIO-Protobuf: hay que convertir un dataset de entrenamiento a RecordIO-Protobuf (para Pipe mode de SageMaker seq2seq). El equipo ya usa EMR Spark para otras cargas. ¿Qué opción es la más adecuada?
options: Desplegar una tarea AWS Fargate con un contenedor propio que haga la conversión del dataset a RecordIO
Montar un clúster EMR, cargar el dataset de S3 y usar Apache Spark para hacer las conversiones necesarias
Usar Amazon Redshift Spectrum para consultar el dataset en S3 y realizar las conversiones al formato requerido
Usar un stream de Firehose para ingerir el dataset desde S3 y transformarlo al formato RecordIO-Protobuf
correct_text: Montar un clúster EMR, cargar el dataset de S3 y usar Apache Spark para hacer las conversiones necesarias
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Clúster EMR con Apache Spark.

El problema: transformar grandes volúmenes a RecordIO-Protobuf; el equipo ya tiene experiencia y pipeline EMR Spark, así que reutilizarlo minimiza fricción.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Spark en EMR procesa datos a escala y, con la librería de serialización protobuf, escribe RecordIO-Protobuf; aprovecha herramientas ya conocidas por el equipo.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Fargate contenedor propio: exige construir y mantener un contenedor a medida; más trabajo que reutilizar EMR.
  • Redshift Spectrum: consulta datos en S3 con SQL; no está pensado para producir RecordIO-Protobuf.
  • Firehose: es ingesta de streaming; no convierte datasets por lotes a RecordIO-Protobuf.
Exam tip RecordIO-Protobuf es el formato compacto para algoritmos built-in de SageMaker en Pipe mode; EMR/Spark lo procesa a escala y, con la librería de serialización protobuf instalada, escribe ese formato (no es un writer nativo out-of-the-box).

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A team is working on a machine learning project that involves training a recommendation model using the Amazon SageMaker seq2seq algorithm. The dataset is stored in Amazon S3. The team currently uses Amazon EMR Spark jobs for its nightly log aggregation and reporting pipeline, which is separate from the ML workflow.

The goal is to convert this training dataset into the RecordIO-Protobuf format, which is required for efficient training with SageMaker Pipe mode.

Which of the following options would be most suitable for this use case?

Deploy an AWS Fargate task that runs a custom containerized application that is responsible for converting the dataset.
Set up an EMR cluster, load the dataset from S3, and leverage Apache Spark to perform the necessary conversions.
Utilize Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the dataset stored in S3 and perform the necessary conversions.
Use a Firehose stream to ingest the dataset from S3 and transform it into RecordIO-Protobuf format.
Incorrect
Apache Spark is a distributed processing framework and programming model that facilitates machine learning, stream processing, and graph analytics with Amazon EMR clusters. Like Apache Hadoop, Spark is an open-source, distributed processing system commonly utilized for big data workloads. However, Spark differs from Hadoop MapReduce in several significant ways. Spark features an optimized directed acyclic graph (DAG) execution engine and actively caches data in memory, enhancing performance, especially for specific algorithms and interactive queries.

Amazon EMR - Apache Spark

Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce) is a managed big data platform that allows you to process large datasets using popular frameworks like Apache Spark.

EMR Cluster: EMR provides a scalable and cost-effective way to process data. You can create an EMR cluster, which automatically provisions the necessary resources (such as EC2 instances) for your Spark jobs.

Spark is a powerful distributed data processing framework. You can write Spark jobs to read the dataset from Amazon S3, transform it into the RecordIO-Protobuf format, and save it back to S3. Spark’s parallel processing capabilities make it efficient for large-scale data conversion.

RecordIO-Protobuf Format: EMR allows you to install additional libraries (such as protobuf) on the cluster, enabling you to serialize your data into the required format.

Hence, the correct answer is: Set up an EMR cluster, load the dataset from S3, and leverage Apache Spark to perform the necessary conversions.

The option that says: Deploy an AWS Fargate task that runs a custom containerized application that is responsible for converting the dataset is incorrect. While Fargate is suitable for running containerized applications, it’s not the most straightforward solution for this specific use case. Setting up a custom containerized application introduces unnecessary complexity. You’d need to manage the container, orchestration, and data transfer.

The option that says: Use a Firehose stream to ingest the dataset from S3 and transform it into RecordIO-Protobuf format is incorrect because a Firehose stream is primarily designed for real-time streaming data delivery, not for batch processing or converting static datasets stored in S3.

The option that says: Utilize Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the dataset stored in S3 and perform the necessary conversions is incorrect. Redshift Spectrum is a query service for analyzing data in S3 using SQL queries. However, it’s not meant for format conversion. Redshift Spectrum is only used for analytical queries rather than data transformation.

question: Faltantes con mínimo overhead: datos de series de tiempo en Redshift con valores faltantes; se quiere una solución totalmente administrada, dentro de SageMaker, para preprocesar. ¿Qué enfoque es el más eficiente operativamente?
options: Preprocesar con las funciones integradas de SageMaker Data Wrangler dentro de SageMaker Canvas
Usar funciones SQL nativas de Redshift para tratar los faltantes dentro del clúster antes de exportar
Exportar de Redshift a S3 y usar Amazon Athena con sentencias CTAS para preprocesar los faltantes
Desarrollar un script propio en AWS Lambda que identifique y rellene automáticamente los valores faltantes
correct_text: Preprocesar con las funciones integradas de SageMaker Data Wrangler dentro de SageMaker Canvas
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - SageMaker Data Wrangler dentro de Canvas.

El problema: preprocesar faltantes de forma administrada y dentro del entorno SageMaker, con mínimo overhead.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Data Wrangler (integrado en Canvas) ofrece transformaciones e imputación de faltantes sin código, todo dentro de SageMaker.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • SQL en Redshift: queda fuera del entorno SageMaker y mezcla la lógica de ML con la base de datos.
  • Athena CTAS en S3: agrega pasos de exportación y otro servicio, fuera de SageMaker; más overhead.
  • Lambda propia: código a medida a mantener; no es una solución administrada dentro de SageMaker.
Exam tip "Preprocesar sin código dentro de SageMaker" = Data Wrangler (en Studio o Canvas).

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A logistics company is optimizing delivery routes using historical time-series data, but faces missing values in its dataset. The training data is stored in Amazon Redshift, and the company plans to implement a fully managed solution for data preprocessing and feature engineering entirely within the Amazon SageMaker AI environment to streamline its complex ML workflows.

What is the MOST operationally efficient way to handle the missing values in its dataset?

Perform data preprocessing using SageMaker Data Wrangler built-in features within SageMaker Canvas to handle missing values.
Use Redshift's built-in SQL functions to handle missing values directly within the Redshift cluster before exporting the unstructured format records to SageMaker AI for model development.

Export the data from Redshift to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) statements to preprocess the data and handle missing values before importing it back into SageMaker AI.
Develop a custom script using AWS Lambda to automatically identify and fill in missing values.
Incorrect
SageMaker Data Wrangler is a feature of Amazon SageMaker AI that accelerates data preparation for machine learning. You can use it to clean, transform, and analyze time-series data quickly. It provides built-in data transformations, including robust methods to handle missing values (such as imputation), to streamline ML workflows. Since it is natively integrated into the SageMaker Canvas workspace, data scientists can perform these preprocessing tasks entirely within the SageMaker environment without writing complex code, making it the most operationally efficient fully managed solution.

amazon-sagemaker-data-wrangler-architecture

Hence, the correct answer is: Perform data preprocessing using SageMaker Data Wrangler built-in features within SageMaker Canvas to handle missing values.

The option that says: Use Redshift’s built-in SQL functions to handle missing values directly within the Redshift cluster before exporting the unstructured format records to SageMaker AI for model development is incorrect because while Amazon Redshift can perform SQL-based data manipulation, processing the data before exporting it breaks the requirement of performing data preprocessing “entirely within the Amazon SageMaker AI environment”. It typically involves more manual effort compared to using SageMaker’s built-in visual tools.

The option that says: Export the data from Redshift to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) statements to preprocess the data and handle missing values before importing it back into SageMaker AI is incorrect because adding Amazon S3 and Amazon Athena into the pipeline increases architecture complexity. Athena is primarily an interactive query service, and using it for robust ML feature engineering and missing value imputation requires custom queries, resulting in higher operational overhead.

The option that says: Develop a custom script using AWS Lambda to automatically identify and fill in missing values is incorrect because AWS Lambda requires custom code development, testing, and maintenance to handle data imputation. This significantly increases operational overhead compared to using the out-of-the-box features provided by SageMaker Data Wrangler.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/canvas-data-preparation.html

question: Redactar PII/PHI en PDFs: registros médicos en PDF en S3; antes de entrenar hay que detectar y redactar PII/PHI de forma operativamente eficiente. ¿Qué solución conviene?
options: Un modelo ready-to-use de SageMaker Canvas que ingiera los PDFs y redacte por sí solo la PII/PHI
Amazon Textract para extraer el texto de los PDFs y Amazon Comprehend para detectar y redactar la PII/PHI
S3 Object Lambda con una función propia que llame a Comprehend y redacte la PII/PHI al leer cada objeto
Amazon Textract para extraer el texto y luego un modelo preentrenado de clasificación de SageMaker JumpStart
correct_text: Amazon Textract para extraer el texto de los PDFs y Amazon Comprehend para detectar y redactar la PII/PHI
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - Amazon Textract (extraer texto del PDF) + Amazon Comprehend (detectar y redactar PII/PHI).

El problema: detectar y redactar PII (datos personales) y PHI (información de salud) en PDFs con el menor esfuerzo operativo. Comprehend solo procesa texto plano, no PDFs.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Amazon Textract extrae el texto de los PDFs y Amazon Comprehend ejecuta un job asíncrono de PII con modo de salida "redacción" (StartPiiEntitiesDetectionJob), que devuelve el texto con cada entidad PII/PHI enmascarada, sin entrenar modelos.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • Modelo ready-to-use de Canvas: el modelo de "detección de información personal" de Canvas solo acepta texto o tabular y únicamente detecta (no redacta) ni procesa PDFs; no cumple el requisito.
  • S3 Object Lambda + función propia: redacta en el momento de la lectura, pero exige desarrollar y mantener la función Lambda y sigue necesitando extraer el texto del PDF; más overhead operativo.
  • Textract + JumpStart: un modelo de clasificación de JumpStart no redacta PII; habría que entrenar o ajustar lógica a medida, más esfuerzo que usar Comprehend.
Exam tip Redactar PII/PHI de documentos = Textract (PDF a texto) + Comprehend (job asíncrono de PII con salida redactada). Canvas ready-to-use detecta, no redacta, y no lee PDFs.

Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
Category: MLA – Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
A healthcare technology company is developing a machine learning model to analyze medical records. These records are in PDF format and stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. These records contain sensitive information such as patient names, addresses, phone numbers, and medical history details. Before training the model, the company must detect and redact personally identifiable information (PII) and protected health information (PHI) from the records to ensure compliance with data privacy regulations.

Which is the most operationally efficient solution that can meet the requirements?

Use a SageMaker Canvas ready-to-use model to process PDFs and redact PII/PHI.
Convert PDFs to text, then use Comprehend to detect and redact PII/PHI.
Use S3 Object Lambda with Comprehend to redact PII/PHI.
Use Amazon Textract to extract text from PDFs, then use a SageMaker JumpStart pre-trained model for redaction.
Incorrect
Amazon SageMaker Canvas is a no-code visual interface that empowers you to prepare data, build, and deploy highly accurate ML models, streamlining the end-to-end ML lifecycle in a unified environment. With SageMaker Canvas, users can easily import data from various sources, visualize and prepare the data, and then train, evaluate, and deploy ML models using a simple drag-and-drop interface. SageMaker Canvas leverages Amazon SageMaker’s robust ML infrastructure to provide an intuitive platform for creating predictive models, making machine learning more accessible to a broader audience, including those without deep technical expertise.



Using Amazon SageMaker Canvas eliminates the need for extensive configuration, manual intervention, or the setup of additional services, thus significantly reducing operational overhead. It includes ready-to-use models that can automatically detect and redact PII and PHI from text data. This solution requires the least operational overhead because you can use a pre-built model without developing your code or converting the PDF files to text format.

Hence, the correct answer is: Use a SageMaker Canvas ready-to-use model to process PDFs and redact PII/PHI.

The option that says: Use S3 Object Lambda with Comprehend to redact PII/PHI is incorrect. While Amazon Comprehend can detect and redact PII and PHI from text data, using it with an Amazon S3 Object Lambda access point would only introduce additional operational overhead. This approach would require configuring, deploying, and maintaining a Lambda function, which goes against the requirement of minimal operational overhead.

The option that says: Convert PDFs to text, then use Comprehend to detect and redact PII/PHI is incorrect. While Amazon Comprehend can primarily detect and redact PII and PHI from text data, it cannot process PDF files directly. The PDF files would need to be converted to text format first, adding operational overhead compared to using a SageMaker Canvas ready-to-use model that can process PDF files directly.

The option that says: Use Amazon Textract to extract text from PDFs, then use a SageMaker JumpStart pre-trained model for redaction is incorrect. While Amazon Textract can extract text from PDF files, and SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained models, this solution requires more operational overhead than a SageMaker Canvas ready-to-use model. You would need to configure and deploy the pre-trained model and integrate it with Amazon Textract.

 

References:

question: Compartir features entre cuentas: varias apps de ML requieren entrenamiento e inferencia de baja latencia y necesitan compartir features entre cuentas AWS con mínimo overhead. ¿Qué opción cumple?
options: Usar SageMaker Feature Store con online y offline store y configurar acceso cross-account para compartir features
Usar Amazon RDS para almacenar features y montar replicación entre bases de datos en distintas cuentas
Guardar las features en Amazon S3 y gestionar manualmente políticas IAM de acceso por cada cuenta involucrada
Guardar en S3 y usar AWS Glue con DynamicFrames para transformar y catalogar, compartiendo luego entre cuentas
correct_text: Usar SageMaker Feature Store con online y offline store y configurar acceso cross-account para compartir features
answer_html:
Correcta: {{L}} - SageMaker Feature Store (online + offline) con acceso cross-account.

El problema: se requiere un repositorio de features con online store (baja latencia para inferencia) y offline store (entrenamiento), compartible entre cuentas.

Por qué la respuesta sirve: Feature Store es el servicio administrado para esto: online para inferencia rápida, offline para entrenamiento, y soporta acceso cross-account con poco overhead.

Por qué NO las otras, una por una:

  • RDS con replicación: no es un feature store; operar replicación entre cuentas es más complejo y sin online/offline nativos.
  • S3 + IAM manual: gestionar políticas por cuenta a mano es mucho overhead y no da online store de baja latencia.
  • S3 + Glue DynamicFrames: es ETL/catálogo, no un feature store con inferencia de baja latencia.
